children: By Callum Keown and Mariapaula Gonzalez
Most stocks turned higher Tuesday afternoon after worries about AI spending eased.

The earlier tech selloff was triggered by the IPO flop of South Korean data-center-infrastructure company Elice. The stock plunged 32% after its trading debut, despite reports that retail demand was 400 times oversubscribed.
Korean memory-chip giant SK Hynix's American depositary receipts fell 2.2%. But the pressure extended to the U.S. tech sector.
Chip stocks end the session slightly lower, erasing their midday rebound.

Micron fell 1% as three warning signals weighed: a potential workers' strike in Taiwan, spillover effect from Elice's disastrous IPO, and broader pressures about the mounting debt required to fund AI infrastructure expansions.
CoreWeave, the poster-child of AI debt fears, was up 1.7%. Shares have fallen nearly 29% this month and 51% over the past year. IREN, another so-called neocloud provider, was down 4%.

Salesforce was roughly flat. The company said Tuesday it would acquire customer engagement platform Braze for about $5.7 billion in enterprise value. Under the agreement, Braze Class A shareholders would receive $47.50 in cash per share, a 58% upside from the closing price of $30.04 from Monday. Shares of Braze surged 52%.
Equifax gained 11% and was the best performer in the S&P 500. The company said U.S. mortgage revenue grew 15% even as the mortgage market weakened on a substantial increase in mortgage rates.

Hasbro was the S&P 500's second best performer, jumping over 11%. The game maker said revenue for Magic: The Gathering, its franchise tabletop and digital game, grew 34% from a year ago to top $600 million in quarterly revenue for the first time.
SpaceX slipped 0.1% ahead of the rocket and AI company's earnings.

Apple declined 1% to $339.50. Loop Capital downgraded the stock to Hold from Buy based on the firm's new iPhone data after Apple reduced its September and December iPhone unit shipments by 10%. The firm also reduced Apple's price target to $330 from $370.

General Motors dropped 6.8%. The Detroit-based auto maker left the midpoint of its full-year operating profit guidance unchanged at $15 billion. Wall Street anticipates that figure to slightly top $15 billion, so management's outlook implies a weaker-than-expected fourth quarter.

GE Aerospace declined 4.7%. Though the company topped Wall Street's estimates, investors looked past the strong earnings and were likely worrying about a potential slowdown in aftermarket growth in 2027.
3M advanced 5.8% after its earnings as the company expanded its date-center products deal with Amazon. Steel Dynamics fell 0.3% after earnings missed estimates late Monday.

Halliburton rose 1.9%. The oilfield services giant outlined preliminary guidance for 2027 and posted an 8% sequential increase in revenue from the Middle East, reversing the previous quarter's sequential decline.
